items.text: Pain abrupt in onset and maximal at onset (thunderclap-type chest/back pain)

citations: Becker T, Kharbanda A, Bachur R. Atypical clinical features of pediatric appendicitis. Acad Emerg Med. 2007;14(2):124-129.
Bundy DG, Byerley JS, Liles EA, Perrin EM, Katznelson J, Rice HE. Does this child have appendicitis? JAMA. 2007;298(4):438-451.
Golledge J, Toms AP, Franklin IJ, Scriven MW, Galland RB. Assessment of peritonism in appendicitis. Ann R Coll Surg Engl. 1996;78(1):11-14.

ask.changes_what: Present: escalate now - CT angiography for suspected mesenteric ischemia; urgent surgical consult for suspected necrotizing infection. Absent: does not lower probability enough to stop work-up.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not apply to patients who cannot report pain reliably (sedation, dementia, spinal cord injury); absence of the sign never excludes either diagnosis.
ask.escalation_warning: Suspected necrotizing infection or mesenteric ischemia is time-critical: surgical consultation / CT angiography without waiting for laboratory results.

evidence.citation: Alayed KA, Tan C, Daneman N. Red Flags for Necrotizing Fasciitis: A Case Control Study. International journal of infectious diseases : IJID : official publication of the International Society for Infectious Diseases. 2016.
evidence.population: All NF cases admitted to a large Canadian tertiary hospital 2004-2013, each matched to two cellulitis controls (retrospective case-control)
evidence.quote: The clinical features that most significantly increased the odds of NF were recent surgery (LR+ 7.0) pain-out-of-proportion (LR+ 4.5), diarrhea (LR+ 6.0)
evidence.reference_standard: Admitted with diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis (chart-confirmed) versus cellulitis controls
evidence.target_condition: Necrotizing fasciitis versus cellulitis (case-control): pain-out-of-proportion documented on history/physical examination

ask.how: Compare reported pain severity and analgesic requirement with objective findings: for the abdomen, severe continuous pain with a soft, non-tender or minimally tender abdomen; for skin/soft tissue, severe pain or exquisite tenderness extending beyond the visible erythema, or pain disproportionate to a modest cellulitis. Record the discordance explicitly.
ask.negative_finding: Absence is not reassuring: no single red flag had sufficient sensitivity to rule out necrotizing fasciitis (LR- >=0.5 for all findings), and mesenteric ischemia frequently presents with vague or non-specific pain, especially in the elderly.
ask.pitfalls: Late presentations of ischemia develop peritonism, so the sign is transient; analgesia, diabetes, and altered mental status blunt reporting. Distinguishing 'out of proportion' is subjective and undefined in most studies.
ask.positive_finding: In a soft-tissue infection, pain out of proportion raised the odds of necrotizing fasciitis about 4.5-fold versus cellulitis in a case-control study; in abdominal pain with vascular risk (AF, atherosclerosis, low flow), it is the classic cue for early mesenteric ischemia and should prompt CT angiography rather than observation.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to report pain; opioid or sedative effect accounted for.
ask.rationale: Pain out of proportion to exam is a key discriminator for mesenteric ischemia, the top differential, and would prompt urgent imaging and surgical consult.
ask.title: Pain out of proportion to examination findings

ask.changes_what: Positive: escalate to ADD-RS assessment, CXR/D-dimer and CT angiography as appropriate; negative onset lowers but does not eliminate dissection probability.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use gradual onset alone to exclude dissection in patients with other high-risk features (Marfan/aortic disease, pulse deficit, neurologic deficit, new murmur, hypotension).
ask.escalation_warning: Abrupt severe chest/back pain with hypotension, pulse deficit, or neurologic deficit is a dissection or ruptured AAA until proven otherwise: immediate CT angiography and surgical notification.

evidence.citation: Klompas M. Does this patient have an acute thoracic aortic dissection? JAMA. 2002;287(17):2262-2272.
evidence.population: Consecutive patients with confirmed thoracic aortic dissection from 21 studies (case series; sensitivity pooled; LR- derived from comparison cohorts)
evidence.quote: sudden onset (sensitivity, 84%). The absence of sudden pain onset lowers the likelihood of dissection (negative likelihood ratio [LR], 0.3; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.2-0.5)
evidence.reference_standard: Dissection confirmed by imaging, surgery, or autopsy
evidence.target_condition: Acute thoracic aortic dissection (finding: sudden-onset pain)

evidence.citation: Ohle R, Um J, Anjum O, et al. High risk clinical features for acute aortic dissection: a case-control study. Acad Emerg Med. 2018;25(4):378-384.
evidence.population: Matched case-control: 194 ED/in-hospital CT- or echo-confirmed AAD cases vs 776 ED controls with truncal pain <14 days and no clear diagnosis
evidence.quote: Absence of abrupt-onset pain (sensitivity = 95.9%, negative likelihood ratio = 0.07 [0.03-0.14]) can help rule out AAD.
evidence.reference_standard: CT angiography or echocardiography confirmed dissection

ask.how: Ask an open question about how the pain began, then specifically: 'Did it reach its worst within seconds, or build up over minutes?' Document time-to-peak intensity and whether the patient can pinpoint the moment of onset (what they were doing). Also ask about tearing/ripping quality and migration.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of sudden onset lowers the likelihood of dissection (LR- 0.3 in the RCE pooled series; 0.07 in an ED case-control study), but the clinical examination is insufficiently sensitive to rule out dissection on its own.
ask.pitfalls: Patients recall onset imprecisely, particularly after analgesia or when pain was preceded by exertion; gradual-onset presentations still occur in ~5-16% of dissections, especially in elderly patients or with painless neurologic presentations.
ask.positive_finding: Abrupt-onset pain is present in ~84-96% of aortic dissections but is common in other conditions, so it raises suspicion for dissection only modestly (specificity not established in unselected cohorts); it is a high-risk feature in the ADD risk score.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give history; otherwise ask witnesses or EMS about onset.
ask.rationale: Abrupt, maximal onset helps distinguish vascular catastrophes like mesenteric ischemia or aortic dissection from other causes.
ask.title: Pain abrupt in onset and maximal at onset (thunderclap-type chest/back pain)

examine.changes_what: Present: treat as peritonitis, obtain surgical review and CT urgently. Absent: modest reassurance only; do not use to withhold imaging.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid deep or repeated palpation once peritonitis is evident.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on absence of guarding to exclude surgical pathology in the elderly, immunosuppressed, obese, pregnant or opioid-treated patient.
examine.escalation_warning: Diffuse rigidity with hypotension or fever is generalized peritonitis until proven otherwise: resuscitate, antibiotics, immediate surgical consultation.

evidence.citation: Becker T, Kharbanda A, Bachur R. Atypical clinical features of pediatric appendicitis. Acad Emerg Med. 2007;14(2):124-129.
evidence.population: 755 children and adolescents (median age 11.9 y) evaluated for suspected appendicitis; 36% had appendicitis
evidence.target_condition: Acute appendicitis (absence of guarding as negative predictor) (pediatric)

evidence.citation: Becker T, Kharbanda A, Bachur R. Atypical clinical features of pediatric appendicitis. Acad Emerg Med. 2007;14(2):124-129.
evidence.population: Children and adolescents with proven appendicitis in the same cohort (n=755 enrolled)

examine.how: With the patient supine, knees flexed and distracted by conversation, palpate each quadrant gently with a flat hand. Involuntary guarding is reflex contraction of the abdominal wall that persists despite relaxation and distraction; rigidity is a board-like wall that does not soften on expiration.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of guarding lowers but does not exclude appendicitis (pediatric LR- ~0.6); early, retrocaecal or perforated disease in the elderly or immunosuppressed may show no guarding.
examine.pitfalls: Voluntary guarding from anxiety, cold hands or ticklishness mimics the sign; obesity, steroids, opioids and advanced age blunt it. Distinguishing voluntary from involuntary guarding is examiner dependent.
examine.positive_finding: Involuntary guarding or rigidity indicates parietal peritoneal irritation (localized or generalized peritonitis) and raises the probability of appendicitis, perforation or other surgical pathology.
examine.prerequisites: Patient able to lie supine and relax; warm hands; examine tender areas last.
examine.rationale: Involuntary guarding or rigidity indicates peritonitis, which would require urgent surgical review and imaging.
examine.title: Involuntary guarding / board-like rigidity

examine.changes_what: Positive: escalate to imaging and surgical review for suspected appendicitis/peritonitis; negative in low-risk patients supports observation, not discharge without follow-up.
examine.contraindications: Avoid in an already rigid, obviously peritonitic abdomen where the manoeuvre adds only pain; prefer percussion or cough tenderness.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a negative result to exclude peritonitis in elderly, immunosuppressed, steroid-treated, obese or obtunded patients, or in pregnancy where the appendix is displaced.
examine.escalation_warning: Generalised rebound with fever, tachycardia or hypotension indicates diffuse peritonitis: resuscitate and obtain immediate surgical review.

evidence.citation: Golledge J, Toms AP, Franklin IJ, Scriven MW, Galland RB. Assessment of peritonism in appendicitis. Ann R Coll Surg Engl. 1996;78(1):11-14.
evidence.population: 100 consecutive patients with right iliac fossa pain, median age 25 (range 4-81), UK surgical unit; 44 histology-proven appendicitis
evidence.quote: Rebound tenderness proved to be sensitive (sensitivity 0.82), specific (specificity 0.89) and accurate (accuracy 86%).
evidence.reference_standard: Histology at operation; non-operated patients followed clinically

evidence.citation: Bundy DG, Byerley JS, Liles EA, Perrin EM, Katznelson J, Rice HE. Does this child have appendicitis? JAMA. 2007;298(4):438-451.
evidence.population: Children <=18 years in whom appendicitis was suspected and evaluation undertaken; pooled from quality level >=3 studies
evidence.quote: rebound tenderness triples the odds of appendicitis (summary LR, 3.0; 95% CI, 2.3-3.9), while its absence reduces the likelihood (summary LR, 0.28; 95% CI, 0.14-0.55)
evidence.reference_standard: Surgical pathology, clinical observation or follow-up

examine.how: Press slowly and deeply with the fingertips over the area of concern (or a remote quadrant), hold, then release abruptly while watching the patient's face. Pain on release greater than on pressure is rebound tenderness. Gentler equivalents: percussion tenderness, or pain on coughing or heel-drop.
examine.negative_finding: Absence lowers the probability of appendicitis (pediatric LR- 0.28) but does not exclude early, retrocaecal or pelvic appendicitis or peritonitis in the elderly and immunosuppressed.
examine.pitfalls: The classic release manoeuvre is painful and non-specific in anxious patients; percussion or cough tenderness gives similar information more gently. False negatives occur with steroids, advanced age, obesity and altered mental status.
examine.positive_finding: Rebound (or percussion/cough) tenderness indicates parietal peritoneal inflammation; in RIF pain it is specific for appendicitis (spec 0.89, sens 0.82 in adults; pediatric LR+ 3.0).
examine.prerequisites: Explain the manoeuvre; give analgesia first (it does not abolish peritoneal signs); perform once, not repeatedly.
examine.rationale: Rebound tenderness is a classic sign of peritoneal irritation and would escalate the need for imaging and surgical evaluation.
examine.title: Rebound tenderness (peritoneal irritation)

examine.changes_what: Distension + pain/vomiting: NG decompression, fluids, CT abdomen. Tense distension with AKI: measure bladder pressure. Suprapubic dullness: bladder scan and catheterize.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not interpret distension in isolation in patients with ascites, pregnancy, or known chronic megacolon; do not use absence of distension to defer imaging when pain is severe or peritoneal signs exist.
examine.escalation_warning: Distension with peritonism, hemodynamic instability, or rising lactate suggests strangulation or perforation: immediate surgical review. Tense abdomen with oliguria: check intra-abdominal pressure.
examine.how: Inspect the supine abdomen from the side and foot of the bed for a protuberant contour, flank bulging and visible loops or peristalsis. Percuss all quadrants: tympany suggests gas-filled bowel (obstruction/ileus), suprapubic dullness a full bladder, flank dullness fluid. Ask the patient whether the belly feels bigger than usual.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of distension makes complete SBO less likely but does not exclude proximal or early obstruction, ischemia or perforation.
examine.pitfalls: Obesity, ascites, pregnancy and chronic constipation mimic or mask distension; a tense abdomen from retention is easily mistaken for obstruction. Percussion note and contour are poorly reproducible between examiners.
examine.positive_finding: New tympanitic distension with pain and vomiting points to small bowel obstruction (RR ~13 vs no distension in the OMGE series); tense distension with oliguria raises abdominal compartment syndrome; suprapubic dullness suggests retention.
examine.prerequisites: Supine patient with abdomen fully exposed; compare with baseline habitus if known.
examine.rationale: Abdominal distension can point toward obstruction or perforation and would change management toward decompression and urgent imaging.
examine.title: Abdominal distension on inspection/percussion

Abrupt, maximal onset helps distinguish vascular catastrophes like mesenteric ischemia or aortic dissection from other causes.
